outcomes.text: Distinguish four non-finite forms and locate the tense feature.
Find overt and silent subjects, their controllers and the relevant C positions.
Recognize non-finite clause functions and compare Type I and Type II complements.

opening.prompt: Which verb carries past tense in “Nora planned to inspect the bridge”?

options.feedback: “Inspect” stays in its stem form after infinitival “to”.
“Planned” is finite. The infinitival group stays the same in “Nora plans to inspect the bridge”.
Infinitival “to” is untensed.

opening.prompt: In “The crew made Ivo wait”, what form is “wait”?

options.feedback: The verb is in the stem form without “to”.
There is no infinitival “to” in this example.
This would have an -ing form such as “waiting”.

opening.prompt: Who is understood to check the maps in “Nia enjoys checking the maps”?

options.feedback: The main subject identifies the person who checks the maps.
The context here identifies a specific person.
Nia controls the silent subject of “checking the maps”.

opening.prompt: In “For Ivo to wait outside seemed unfair”, who is the overt subject of “to wait”?

options.feedback: “Ivo” occurs inside the clause introduced by “for”.
“For” introduces the clause and “Ivo” is its overt subject.

options.text: The person who thought it unfair
options.feedback: The sentence gives the person who waits, without naming who judged it unfair.

opening.prompt: In “Nia paused to check the ropes”, what gives the purpose of pausing?

options.feedback: The entire infinitival clause gives the purpose.
Nia is the subject of the main clause.
This is the object inside the clause that gives the purpose.

closing.prompt: In “All Ren did was tighten the bolts”, where does [-tense] appear in the bare infinitival VP?

options.feedback: “Was” is finite and outside the bare infinitival VP.
The bare infinitive marks the lexical verb directly.
“Tighten” is the untensed lexical verb.

closing.prompt: In “Mina agreed to count the crates”, where does [-tense] appear in the infinitival VP?

options.feedback: “Count” stays in the stem form. Look at the branch above “to”.
“Count the crates” is the lexical VP complement of “to”.
“Agreed” carries past tense in the main clause.

closing.prompt: In “Reading maps takes practice”, what does the silent subject of “reading” refer to?

options.feedback: There is no overt controller in this sentence.

options.text: A particular person named in the sentence
options.feedback: No person is named.
“Maps” is what people read, so it is the object.

closing.prompt: Compare “They expected Lea to sing” and “They persuaded Lea to sing”. In which is “Lea” the overt subject inside the infinitival clause?

options.feedback: Lea is understood to sing in both, but only one has her name inside the lower clause.
Lea is the higher object in this sentence. She controls the silent lower subject.
The whole clause “Lea to sing” is the complement of “expected”.

closing.prompt: In “Mina insisted on locking the gate”, what is the function of “locking the gate”?

options.feedback: “Mina” is the main subject.
The -ing clause is the group selected by the preposition.
The clause supplies what Mina insisted on.
